summary: Leaders made their final pitches to Albertans before Monday's referendum, with over a million ballots already cast. Monday also brings new inflation numbers before the Bank of Canada's Oct. 28 rate decision.
body: Alberta votes Monday, and the last push came Friday. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre spoke in Calgary, saying he understands frustration with Ottawa over costs, crime, immigration and resource policy, but that leaving is not the answer. "Albertans are not quitters," he said [^1]. Prime Minister Mark Carney appeared with Premier Danielle Smith in Red Deer, then ended a two-day Alberta tour with a rally in Edmonton, his hometown, where he called a vote to leave a "dangerous bluff" [^2]. Smith says she will vote to remain [^2]. Question 10 asks whether Alberta should stay in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on separating [^1][^2].

Early voting has been heavy. More than one million ballots were cast by Thursday, about a third of roughly three million eligible voters, and advance polls close Saturday evening [^2][^3]. A new Angus Reid poll (Oct. 13-15) puts remain at 66% and secession at 34%; most people leaning toward secession told the pollster they mainly want to send Ottawa a message [^3]. My read: pollsters say high turnout tends to help the remain side, but the result on Monday night is what counts.

On the economy, Statistics Canada releases September inflation numbers on Monday, and the Bank of Canada publishes its quarterly business and consumer surveys the same day [^4]. Both feed into the bank's Oct. 28 interest-rate decision. An RBC economist expects inflation stayed near 3% because of gas prices and calls the meeting "live" (meaning a rate hike is possible), though not his base case [^4]. Interest rates affect what families pay on loans and mortgages. Otherwise, a quiet couple of days for Ontario politics.
differences: Not everyone thinks the big rallies help. Former premier Jason Kenney said federalist rallies may backfire, pointing to Quebec's 1995 referendum, though he hopes they boost turnout [^2]. Critics say Smith gave fringe separatist ideas a platform by calling the vote; she says she backs remaining [^1][^2]. An Abacus Data poll done for the Alberta Federation of Labour found 56% think the referendum should not be held at all [^2].
